section.title: A Lament over Tyre
section.sectionRationale: Having pronounced Tyre's sentence, Ezekiel is now told to take up a lament for her, singing as though at a funeral for a great ship. The chapter catalogs Tyre's builders, crews, soldiers, and trading partners from every corner of the known world in loving, almost admiring detail, only to sink that whole magnificent vessel in a single verse, showing how suddenly all that glory comes to nothing.
section.thesis: Tyre's beauty, wealth, and worldwide trade, described here in exquisite and lingering detail, cannot save her when the LORD's judgment comes; the very splendor that made her proud becomes the cargo that sinks with her into the heart of the sea.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Tyre pictured as a magnificent ship, perfect in beauty and built from the finest materials of many lands; her vast network of trading partners spanning the known world; and the sudden wreck of that whole glorious vessel, mourned by sailors and kings alike.

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Now you, son of man, take up a lament for Tyre.
Tell Tyre, who dwells at the gateway to the sea, merchant of the peoples on many coasts, that this is what the Lord GOD says: You have said, O Tyre, 'I am {{kalil|perfect in beauty}}.'
Your borders are in the heart of the seas; your builders perfected your beauty.
They constructed all your planking with cypress from Senir. They took a cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you.
Of oaks from Bashan they made your oars; of wood from the coasts of Cyprus they made your deck, inlaid with ivory.
Of embroidered fine linen from Egypt they made your sail, which served as your banner. Of blue and purple from the coasts of Elishah they made your awning.
The men of Sidon and Arvad were your oarsmen. Your men of skill, O Tyre, were there as your captains.
The elders of Gebal were aboard as shipwrights, repairing your leaks. All the ships of the sea and their sailors came alongside to barter for your merchandise.
Men of Persia, Lydia, and Put served as warriors in your army. They hung their shields and helmets on your walls; they gave you splendor.
Men of Arvad and Helech manned your walls all around, and the men of Gammad were in your towers. They hung their shields around your walls; they perfected your beauty.

units.label: Merchant of the peoples
units.note: trading partners from every corner of the earth

verses.text: Tarshish was your merchant because of your great wealth of goods; they exchanged silver, iron, tin, and lead for your wares.
Javan, Tubal, and Meshech were your merchants. They exchanged slaves and bronze utensils for your merchandise.
The men of Beth-togarmah exchanged horses, war horses, and mules for your wares.
The men of Dedan were your clients; many coastlands were your market; they paid you with ivory tusks and ebony.
Aram was your customer because of your many products; they exchanged turquoise, purple, embroidered work, fine linen, coral, and rubies for your wares.
Judah and the land of Israel traded with you; they exchanged wheat from Minnith, cakes and honey, oil and balm for your merchandise.
Because of your many products and your great wealth of goods, Damascus traded with you wine from Helbon, wool from Zahar,
and casks of wine from Izal for your wares. Wrought iron, cassia, and sweet cane were exchanged for your merchandise.
Dedan was your merchant in saddlecloths for riding.
Arabia and all the princes of Kedar were your customers, trading in lambs, rams, and goats.
The merchants of Sheba and Raamah traded with you; for your wares they exchanged gold, the finest of all spices, and precious stones.
Haran, Canneh, and Eden traded with you, and so did the merchants of Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad.
In your marketplace they traded with you fine garments of blue, embroidered work, and multicolored rugs with cords tightly twisted and knotted.
The ships of Tarshish carried your merchandise. And you were filled with heavy cargo in the heart of the sea.

units.label: Wrecked in the heart of the sea

verses.text: Your oarsmen have brought you onto the high seas, but the {{ruach-qadim|east wind}} will shatter you in the heart of the sea.

Your wealth, wares, and merchandise, your sailors, captains, and shipwrights, your merchants and all the warriors within you, with all the other people on board, will sink into the heart of the sea on the day of your downfall.
The countryside will shake when your sailors cry out.
All who handle the oars will abandon their ships. The sailors and all the captains of the sea will stand on the shore.
They will raise their voices for you and cry out bitterly. They will throw dust on their heads and roll in ashes.
They will shave their heads for you and wrap themselves in sackcloth. They will weep over you with anguish of soul and bitter mourning.
As they wail and mourn over you, they will take up a {{qinah|lament}} for you: 'Who was ever like Tyre, silenced in the middle of the sea?
When your wares went out to sea, you satisfied many nations. You enriched the kings of the earth with your abundant wealth and merchandise.
Now you are shattered by the seas in the depths of the waters; your merchandise and the people among you have gone down with you.
All the people of the coastlands are appalled over you. Their kings shudder with fear; their faces are contorted.
Those who trade among the nations hiss at you; you have come to a horrible end and will be no more.'”

kalil.gloss: Complete, perfect, or whole. Tyre's own boast, 'I am perfect in beauty,' claims a completeness that belongs to God alone; the lament exposes how a beauty built purely from trade, timber, and craftsmanship cannot ultimately hold together against judgment.

ruach-qadim.gloss: The east wind, a hot, destructive wind that in the Old Testament often pictures God's own judgment blowing against human pride, as it dries up Egypt's plague relief in Exodus or scatters Israel's leaders in Jeremiah; here it wrecks Tyre's ship at the very height of her voyage.

qinah.gloss: A funeral dirge or lament, the same poetic form used to mourn the dead. This entire chapter is framed as a qinah for Tyre, sung as though for a person, or a great ship, that has died rather than merely a city that has fallen.

basic.context: This chapter follows directly on Tyre's sentence in chapter 26 with an extended, almost loving description of her glory, pictured as a magnificent trading ship built from the finest materials of Lebanon, Bashan, Cyprus, and Egypt, crewed by skilled sailors from Sidon and Arvad, and supplied by merchants from every corner of the known world, before that whole vessel is suddenly wrecked and sinks in a few devastating verses.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a literal historical description of Tyre's real Mediterranean trading network, cast in the poetic form of a lament for the dead, meant to be sung or recited as a dirge rather than delivered as plain prose. The detailed cargo lists describe genuine ancient trade routes and partners; the point of the passage is not merely economic history but the theological lesson that even the most impressive, far reaching human achievement cannot outlast God's judgment.
basic.originalLanguages: Tyre boasts that she is kalil, perfect or complete, a completeness that properly belongs to God alone. Her downfall comes at the hand of the ruach qadim, the east wind, a recurring biblical picture of God's own judgment blowing against human pride. And the whole chapter is framed as a qinah, a funeral lament, treating Tyre's fall with the weight and grief normally reserved for the death of a person.
basic.typology: The ship 'perfect in beauty,' built from the finest materials of many nations yet unable to survive the wind of judgment, anticipates the wider biblical pattern of merchant Babylon in Revelation 18, whose fall is mourned in strikingly similar language by kings, merchants, and sailors, showing that no worldly system of trade and wealth, however global, escapes final judgment before Christ's return.
basic.christ: Tyre's self sufficient boast, 'I am perfect in beauty,' apart from God, is answered by the God who alone truly gives and sustains beauty, wisdom, and stability; where Tyre's borrowed splendor sinks in a moment, Christ offers a kingdom that, unlike Tyre's, 'cannot be shaken,' Hebrews 12:28, built not on trade routes but on His own finished work.
basic.god: God is sovereign not only over armies but over trade, wealth, and the whole interconnected economy of the ancient world; He can name every trading partner, every cargo, every craftsman's homeland, and still bring the entire enterprise down with a single wind, showing His intimate knowledge of and authority over even the most complex human systems.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 23 gives an earlier oracle against Tyre focused on her trade and profit. Revelation 18:9-19 echoes this chapter's precise imagery, merchants, kings, and sailors weeping over a fallen trading empire, applied there to Babylon. Jeremiah 18:17 and Job 27:21 use the same east wind image for sudden, devastating judgment. James 4:13-16 warns against boasting in tomorrow as though wealth and plans were guaranteed, a New Testament echo of Tyre's presumption.
basic.oneStory: Tyre's glittering, worldwide trade could not save her from the wind of judgment, and her fall is mourned as though a great ship, even a person, had died. This anticipates the whole Bible's pattern that every impressive human achievement, apart from God, will finally sink, while the kingdom built on Christ alone remains when every other splendor has gone down into the sea.

context.literary:
Chapter 27 is one extended metaphor, and the metaphor is sustained to the end. Tyre is a ship. The chapter is introduced as a qinah, a funeral lament, verse 2, and it behaves like one: the funeral song begins with the splendor of the dead, and only in its last third does the death arrive. The three movements are the building of the ship, verses 3 to 11, the filling of the ship with cargo, verses 12 to 25, and the wrecking of the ship, verses 26 to 36. The middle section is the longest and the slowest, a list that runs like a ship's manifest.

The hinge between the second and third movements is verse 25. The same sentence that ends the cargo list, 'you were filled with heavy cargo in the heart of the sea', begins the disaster, for the ship is overloaded and the storm is waiting. The phrase 'heart of the seas' appears in verses 4, 25, 26 and 27. It first marks Tyre's proud position, her borders 'in the heart of the seas', and by verse 27 it marks the place where everything sinks. A place of glory becomes a place of burial through repetition of the same words.

There is a careful pairing of beauty and ruin. In verse 3 Tyre says she is 'perfect in beauty', in verses 4 and 11 her builders 'perfected' it. In verse 4 the beauty is built by human hands, a quiet argument against the boast of verse 3. Then in the last section the same sailors who steered the ship stand on the shore and weep.

Notice who mourns. In verses 28 to 32 it is not Tyre's citizens but the oarsmen, the captains, the sailors, and the coastlands. They mourn the loss of a trading hub. Verse 32 then quotes their own lament inside the lament, 'Who was ever like Tyre?', and verse 36 closes with a hiss. The lament is for a market, and the market's friends hiss when it is gone.
context.historical:
Phoenician sailors were the long-distance traders of the ancient Mediterranean, and Tyre was their greatest city. What Ezekiel gives is a world map seen from Tyre's quay. The ship's materials come from all over the known world: cypress from Senir, which is Mount Hermon, a cedar mast from Lebanon, oak oars from Bashan, an ivory-inlaid deck from the coasts of Cyprus, linen sails from Egypt, and purple awnings from Elishah. These are the best materials from the best sources, and the verse is itself a catalogue of the places that fed the Tyrian economy.

The crew list is equally international. Rowers come from Sidon and Arvad, shipwrights from Gebal, and the army from Persia, Lydia and Put. Tyre did not rely on its own people for its defence. It hired its strength, and hung the foreign shields on its walls as ornaments, verses 10 to 11.

The cargo list in verses 12 to 24 names more than twenty trading partners, from Tarshish at the far western end of the Mediterranean to Sheba in southern Arabia, and from Judah and Israel to Damascus, Kedar, Asshur and Haran. Silver, iron, tin and lead come from the west, horses and mules from the north, ivory and ebony from Africa, spices and gold from Arabia, and wine and wool from Damascus. In verse 17 Judah and Israel supply wheat, oil, honey and balm. The land the LORD gave His people fed the city that would gloat over their fall, a detail the first hearers would have felt, since 1 Kings 5:9 to 11 and Acts 12:20 show the same dependence at other periods.

The cargo includes human beings. Verse 13 lists slaves among the exports to Javan, Tubal and Meshech. Joel 3:6 says Tyre sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks, who are the sons of Javan, so this is not a general footnote but the hint of a charge.

The text also has uncertainties. A footnote at verse 15 says the Hebrew reads Dedan while the Septuagint reads Rhodes, and at verse 16 some manuscripts read Edom for Aram. The passage is a work of detailed geography, and scribes have stumbled over some of its names.
context.canonical:
The lament is a recognised form with a long history. David sang one over Saul and Jonathan, 'How the mighty have fallen', 2 Samuel 1:19, and Jeremiah and the author of Lamentations carried the form into the destruction of Jerusalem. Ezekiel uses it on Israel's princes, 19:1, on the king of Tyre, 28:12, and on Pharaoh, 32:2. Here he turns it on a pagan trading city, and the staple mourners, the sailors and merchants, are themselves part of the poem.

The list of nations is deliberately biblical. A great many of the names echo the table of nations in Genesis 10: Javan, Tubal and Meshech, Tarshish, Elishah, Put, Sheba and Dedan, Asshur, and the Sidonians and Arvadites among Canaan's descendants. Tyre's trade shows the scattered peoples of Genesis 10 and 11 brought together again, not by obedience to God but by commerce.

Several texts supply the sea-wreck pattern. Psalm 48:7 says, 'With a wind from the east You wrecked the ships of Tarshish', and Isaiah 23:1 tells the ships of Tarshish to wail. Revelation 18 takes up the whole of this chapter. Merchants of the earth weep because no one buys their cargo, and the cargo list in 18:12 to 13 reads like Ezekiel 27 updated, gold, silver, precious stones, fine linen, purple, ivory, bronze, iron, wine, oil, wheat, horses, and finally 'slaves and souls of men'. Shipmasters and sailors stand at a distance, and they 'throw dust on their heads', Revelation 18:17 to 19, just as the sailors in Ezekiel 27:29 to 30 do.

The chapter also has gentler echoes. Isaiah 60:6 to 9 sees Sheba, Kedar, and the ships of Tarshish bringing gifts to Zion, the same trading partners now turned toward worship. Jesus' warning, 'What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?', Matthew 16:26, and James 4:13 to 16 speak to the same love of business planning without God.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel wants his hearers to see how splendid Tyre was before they see her sink. That is deliberate. If the poem began with her wreck, the exiles might think her fall was simply bad luck, or that her wealth was a minor matter. By lingering over the beauty, the craftsmanship and the cargo, the prophet takes his hearers into Tyre's own view of herself, 'I am perfect in beauty', and lets them feel its pull. Then he lets the wind blow.

The first intent is a warning against being dazzled. Jerusalem herself had been 'perfect' in beauty, Ezekiel 16:14, and had trusted in it. Tyre is a mirror for the exiles. They had watched a city they thought invulnerable fall, and here is another one, richer and more secure by any measure, whose security is equally empty.

The second intent is a theological point about wealth. Everything on the ship was received: cedar, linen, silver, skill. The chapter lists the gifts of many hands. What Tyre did wrong was to describe all of it as her own perfection. The prophet wants God's people to say 'thanks' where Tyre said 'mine'.

The third intent is to show that no network of alliances is a refuge. Tyre's partners, her hired soldiers and her trade routes all go down with her, and her friends stand on the shore and watch. The exiles, who had once looked to Egypt and other allies for help, should hear this and put their weight on the LORD alone.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes Tyre's trade and her ruin. It does not command a particular economic system, and it does not condemn commerce. The ship is built by skilled hands, and the text treats the craft with evident respect. What the passage opposes is the heart that takes the gifts and says 'perfect in beauty' of itself.

Careful readers should also resist the move of turning the passage into a map of present-day nations or trade blocs. The names belong to the sixth century BC. The cargo list is history and poetry, not a code. Its application is to the attitude it exposes, and Revelation 18 shows the New Testament doing exactly that, taking the form but applying it to a larger power.

What the chapter does prescribe, by implication, is the right use of wealth and skill. It shows mourners who grieve for lost profit rather than for people, and a trade that includes the buying and selling of human beings, verse 13. These details are held up as warnings. Believers are to work, trade and build, but to refuse the sale of people, to deal honestly, and to remember, as James puts it, that 'you are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes', James 4:14.

debates.question: Why does Ezekiel describe Tyre's glory in such loving, extensive, almost admiring detail, twenty five verses of careful cargo lists and craftsmanship, before her fall, rather than moving quickly to judgment?

views.label: The extended praise heightens the tragedy and the lesson of the lament form
views.case: A qinah, a funeral lament, traditionally recalls the full glory and virtues of the deceased before mourning the loss; the lingering, admiring detail is not approval of Tyre's pride but a deliberate literary technique making her sudden, total collapse feel as devastating to the reader as it would to those who depended on her.

views.label: The detail shows God's genuine appreciation for human skill and craftsmanship, judged only where it turns to pride
views.case: The passage's warmth toward Tyre's genuinely impressive shipbuilding, trade networks, and artisanship reflects that such skill is itself a good gift, reflecting the image of a creative God; the judgment falls not on craftsmanship or trade as such but on the self sufficient boast, 'I am perfect in beauty,' that forgot the giver of every skill being described.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm that the passage does not condemn skill, trade, or beauty themselves; the tragedy is that such genuine goods were finally trusted in for their own sake rather than received with gratitude toward the God who gives every skilled hand its ability.

debates.question: Is the catalogue of trading partners a precise record of Tyre's actual commerce, or a literary construction?

views.label: A faithful historical record
views.case: The goods match what is known of the ancient Mediterranean: tin and silver from the far west, iron and bronze from Anatolia, horses from the northern highlands, spices and gold from Arabia. The details are specific, such as wine from Helbon and wool from Zahar in verse 18, and the Hebrew prophet had no reason to invent them. Ezekiel was among exiles in Babylon, which had trade connections that could have supplied him with such lists.

views.label: A deliberately shaped and idealised catalogue
views.case: Many names draw on the table of nations in Genesis 10, the list of partners is arranged in a literary pattern, and the manuscripts disagree about several names, verses 15, 16 and 19. On this view the prophet has built a symbolic map of the whole world flowing to Tyre, and the list is as much a portrait of Tyre's pride as a ledger of her accounts.

debates.bearing: The two views are not strictly opposed. Even a literary shaping would work with real trade. Either way the point of the list is theological, that all the world's wealth gathered in one ship and could not save it.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with the phrase 'heart of the seas', in Hebrew lev yammim, which appears in verses 4, 25, 26 and 27. 'Heart' here means the middle, the innermost place. Tyre's boast is that she sits at the heart of the sea. The same word 'heart', lev, is the one used for the ruler's proud inner life in Ezekiel 28:2 and 28:5. The vocabulary of physical and moral centre is shared: the city with its heart in the sea, and the ruler with a proud heart. In verse 25 the verb behind 'heavy cargo' comes from a root that gives both 'heavy' and, in its noun form, 'glory'. The ship is glorious in the sense of weighty, and the weight sinks her.

Verse 7 says the Egyptian linen sail 'served as your banner', using the Hebrew nes, the word for a standard or signal pole. The sail is a flag, announcing the ship's identity to every harbour. Even her sail is advertising. That detail is often missed in translation, but it carries the chapter's theme of display.

In verse 13 the BSB renders a trade item as 'slaves'. The Hebrew idiom is literally 'souls of men', a phrase that Revelation 18:13 takes into Greek as 'souls of men', psychas anthropon. Tyre's cargo includes human lives, and the identical wording in Revelation shows the New Testament reader of Ezekiel noticed it. Joel 3:6 gives the same business a name, selling the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks.

The 'Tarshish' ships of verse 25 are a puzzle for the translator. The BSB gives 'ships of Tarshish' and notes the alternative 'a fleet of trading ships'. In the Old Testament 'ship of Tarshish' became the term for a large ocean-going merchant vessel, 1 Kings 10:22 and Isaiah 23:1, so the translator has to choose between a place and a type. That also explains how Psalm 48:7 can describe the LORD wrecking 'the ships of Tarshish' with an east wind.

The lament in verse 32 is in the same qinah form as verse 2. Look at its question, 'Who was ever like Tyre?' At the Red Sea Israel sang a similar question of God alone, asking who among the gods is like the LORD, Exodus 15:11. The mourners' question borrows that form for a city, and the true answer to it is the LORD.

Finally, the closing word of verse 36 is a hiss, sharaq. It is the sound made at a ruin, as in Jeremiah 19:8. The trading partners who once bowed to Tyre's prosperity hiss at her fall. The last sound of the chapter is the sound of fair-weather friends.

typology.type: The ship wrecked in the heart of the sea, Ezekiel 27:26-27
typology.fulfillment: Tyre's ship, overloaded and exposed to the east wind, sinks with all her cargo, crew and warriors. The pattern is taken up in Revelation 18, where the great city is cast into the sea like a millstone, Revelation 18:21. The escalation is that the city is no longer one port but the whole system of world commerce that opposes God's people, and her destruction is final. The type falls short because Tyre's ruin was an event in history, whereas Revelation's Babylon is a larger symbol, and John names her fall as the end of every such empire.

typology.type: The east wind that shatters the ship, Ezekiel 27:26
typology.fulfillment: The east wind is the LORD's instrument, as at the sea in Exodus 14:21 and in Psalm 48:7. In Christ, a storm breaks over another boat, and the One who sends the wind of judgment rebukes it, Mark 4:39. The boat holds because the Lord is in it. The correspondence is that the wind and sea answer one voice. The escalation is that those who are in Christ's boat are brought through. The type is limited, because Tyre's storm was a judgment and Mark's storm was a test.

typology.type: The mourners on the shore, Ezekiel 27:29-32
typology.fulfillment: Sailors weep, throw dust on their heads and roll in ashes over Tyre. In Revelation 18:9 to 19 kings, merchants and shipmasters do the same over Babylon, and they stand at a distance. Their grief is for lost income, and they say, 'In a single hour she has been destroyed.' Against it stands the heaven's reaction in Revelation 19:1 to 2, the great multitude shouting praise at God's true judgments. The pattern shows two responses to a fallen empire, mourning by those who profited and rejoicing by those who were wronged. It falls short as a prediction, because Ezekiel gives the first and Revelation shows both.

typology.type: Tyre's trading partners brought to Zion, Ezekiel 27:12-25
typology.fulfillment: The nations that carried their goods to Tyre are the nations that Isaiah 60:6 to 9 sees streaming to Zion: Sheba with gold and frankincense, Kedar's flocks, the ships of Tarshish in the lead 'to the honor of the LORD your God'. The same routes, the same peoples and the same wealth are redirected from a proud city to the house of God. Revelation 21:24 says the kings of the earth will bring their glory into the new Jerusalem. The correspondence is that what Tyre gathered for herself is gathered for God. The type falls short in that Tyre's list was a trade, and Zion's is worship.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ by contrast first, and then by a promise hidden inside the list itself.

The contrast is between two kinds of fullness. Tyre is 'filled with heavy cargo', verse 25, and goes down. Christ is the one in whom God was pleased to have 'all His fullness' dwell, Colossians 1:19, and 'from His fullness we have all received grace upon grace', John 1:16. Tyre's boast is 'I am perfect in beauty'; the true beauty is in the Son, who is 'the radiance of God's glory', Hebrews 1:3. Tyre received materials from the world and said they were her own. Christ received everything from the Father and gave it away, Philippians 2:6 to 8.

The second link is Christ's own words about profit. 'What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?' Matthew 16:26. The chapter is a dramatized version of that question, with every cargo of the world on board and the soul of the city lost. His parable of the rich man who built bigger barns and was told, 'You fool! This very night your life will be required of you', Luke 12:16 to 21, tells the same story at the scale of one man. The warning is not against wealth but against being 'not rich toward God', Luke 12:21.

The third link is Christ's mastery of the sea. The east wind in verse 26 is the LORD's. In Mark 4:39 Jesus rebukes the wind and sea, and the disciples ask who this is. Ezekiel 27 shows the LORD wrecking a ship; Mark shows Jesus saving one. The identification is not a coded allegory but a matter of what only God does, since Psalm 89:9 says, 'You rule the raging sea.'

Finally, the Christ who is the end of this chapter's story is the One who offers a kingdom 'unshakable', Hebrews 12:27 to 28. Tyre's world was shaken and sank. Believers are given a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and the right response to it is gratitude and worship.

A caution: Tyre is not a portrait of Christ and the ship is not a picture of the church in Ezekiel. The link is the way the New Testament picks up the chapter's themes of cargo, sea, wealth and soul and sets Christ over them.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who knows the economy of the world in detail. The prophet names forests, ports, metals and animals, and the LORD speaks through him as one who sees the whole system at once. Nothing in the trade of the ancient world was hidden from Him, from the cypress of Hermon to the tin of Tarshish. The doctrine of omniscience is here not abstract but economic: He knows what is bought and sold, and from whom.

He is the giver behind the gifts. Every item on the ship is a created thing: the cedar grew, the flocks bred, the silver lay in the ground. Scripture says that 'the earth is the LORD's, and the fullness thereof', Psalm 24:1, and that it is He who 'gives you the power to gain wealth', Deuteronomy 8:18. Tyre's sin was not to build with these things but to claim them. The chapter honours God by showing His creation to be so abundant that one city could hold the world's goods.

He is sovereign over wind and sea. The same east wind that parts the water for Israel in Exodus 14:21 breaks the ship of Tyre in verse 26. The wind is neither random nor neutral. It obeys the God who made it, and the ship's size, strength and skilled crew do nothing against it. The doctrine of providence reaches even the instruments of business.

He is just. The judgment is not on skill or trade but on a posture, and on the part of the trade that bought and sold persons. The sale of 'souls of men' is not named as a sin in Ezekiel 27 but it is listed, and elsewhere the prophets say the LORD takes it personally, Joel 3:4 to 8.

He is also grieved at ruin that He ordains, and the lament form itself teaches this. God commands Ezekiel to sing a funeral song for a city under sentence. It is not delight in judgment but sober mourning at the end of something that could have been good. Ezekiel 18:23 says God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.

For worship, the chapter calls us to hold wealth and ability with open hands, as received gifts to be used before God. It also calls us to wonder, as the sailors do, at how quickly a world of cargo disappears, and to rest in the God whose kingdom stays when the ships have gone down.

crossReferences.note: Passersby ask of Jerusalem, 'Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty?' Tyre's boast in Ezekiel 27:3 uses the same language of perfect beauty. Jerusalem heard that praise and fell, and the echo shows the prophet making the two cities mirrors of one another.

Of Jerusalem the LORD says her beauty 'was perfect in the splendor I bestowed on you'. The qualification is the difference. Jerusalem's beauty was a gift, and Tyre's boast treats it as her own, which is the issue that the lament of chapter 27 exposes.

'With a wind from the east You wrecked the ships of Tarshish.' It is the closest verbal parallel to Ezekiel 27:25 to 26 and shows the east wind as a recognised tool of divine judgment on the great merchant fleets of the ancient world.

The LORD charges Tyre with selling the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks. Ezekiel 27:13 lists Javan among Tyre's customers for slaves, so the two texts read together make a historical claim that Tyre's wealth included the profit of trading in God's people.

Names such as Javan, Tubal, Meshech, Put, Sheba and Dedan appear in the table of nations. Tyre's trade network in Ezekiel 27 is therefore also a map of the scattered families of Genesis, gathered by commerce rather than by worship of God.

John's lament over Babylon runs through the same cargoes, the same mourning merchants and shipmasters, and the same sudden fall. Revelation 18:13 even closes the cargo list with 'souls of men', as Ezekiel 27:13 does. The chapter is a template for how the New Testament speaks of the final fall of oppressive wealth.

Sheba, Kedar and the ships of Tarshish, all partners of Tyre in Ezekiel 27, appear here bringing gold, flocks and children to Zion for the honour of the LORD. The same people and routes are redirected from a proud city to God's house.

'How the mighty have fallen!' David's lament for Saul and Jonathan is the first great qinah in the Old Testament. Ezekiel 27:32 is the same form and the same cry, now sung for a trading city, and it shows how a human sorrow song can be used to announce a divine judgment.

Jesus rebukes the wind and sea, and the disciples ask who He is. The east wind in Ezekiel 27:26 belongs to the LORD and shatters a ship. Mark 4 shows the same authority over wind and sea in Christ, but used to save, which makes the question 'Who is this?' a question about His identity.

A rich man fills his barns and is told, 'You fool! This very night your life will be required of you.' It is Tyre's story at the scale of one man, a life filled with cargo and empty before God, and it states plainly what Ezekiel 27 shows in parable.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a good creation and a gift: God fills the earth and entrusts it to people to work and to keep, Genesis 1:28 and 2:15. Ezekiel 27 shows what that commission becomes when it is cut off from the Giver. Human skill, the sea, the timber and the metals are exactly what Genesis gave to humanity. The ship of Tyre is a dazzling picture of what people can do with creation, and the lament is the account of what happens when it is done for ourselves.

The chapter also continues Babel's story. Genesis 11 scatters the nations because they sought a name for themselves. Ezekiel 27 shows the nations gathered again, not by a tower but by a market, in a single ship. The same drive towards unity apart from God appears, and the same result, scattering. Revelation 18 will name the end of that line.

It speaks to the exiles' question, too. They had seen Judah's trade and its few allies fail, and had seen Egypt's help prove empty. Chapter 27 tells them that the greatest network of the age cannot hold up against the LORD's wind. The call is to place their hope where wealth cannot reach it.

The story then moves forward in Christ. Jesus warns about the whole world gained and the soul lost, Matthew 16:26, calms a sea, Mark 4:39, and tells people to seek first the kingdom, Matthew 6:33. The early church, in Revelation, receives the vision of Babylon's fall as comfort for believers who are pressed by an empire's economy, and are told to 'come out of her', Revelation 18:4.

The new creation completes it. The sea itself is gone, Revelation 21:1, and the nations bring their glory into the city whose gates are never shut, Revelation 21:24 to 26. The wealth of the world, once spent on one proud ship, is brought home to its Maker. Tyre's trade, redeemed, becomes worship, and her partners, Sheba and Tarshish, come with gifts to the Lord, Isaiah 60:6 to 9.

quiz.q: How is Tyre pictured throughout most of this chapter?

options.text: As a magnificent trading ship, built from the finest materials of many nations and crewed by skilled sailors and craftsmen.
options.note: Verses 4 to 11 describe her planking, mast, oars, sail, and crew all drawn from named regions, forming this extended ship metaphor.

options.text: As a fortified mountain city under siege.
options.note: This chapter's central image is a ship, not a mountain fortress; the siege imagery belongs to chapter 26.

options.text: As a single powerful king ruling alone.
options.note: The focus here is on Tyre's collective trade and craftsmanship, not a single ruler; the king of Tyre is addressed separately in chapter 28.

options.text: As a barren wilderness overtaken by wild animals.
options.note: The dominant image is a glorious, richly furnished ship, not a desolate wilderness.

quiz.q: What does the long list of trading partners in verses 12 to 25 emphasize?

options.text: The vast, worldwide scale of Tyre's commercial network, reaching from Tarshish to Sheba to Javan.
options.note: The list names partners from Spain to Arabia to Asia Minor, underscoring truly global reach for the ancient world.

options.text: That Tyre traded only with her immediate neighbors.
options.note: The opposite is true; the list spans an extraordinarily wide geographic range of partners.

options.text: That Tyre's trade was entirely illegal under international law.
options.note: No legal judgment on the trade itself is made in this list; it simply catalogs partners and goods.

options.text: That Tyre's economy depended on a single trading partner.
options.note: The list names many distinct partners and goods, showing broad diversification, not dependence on one source.

quiz.q: What causes Tyre's sudden downfall in verse 26?

options.text: The east wind shatters her in the heart of the sea.
options.note: Verse 26 names the east wind directly as the force that wrecks her at the height of her voyage.

options.text: A slow decline in trade over many decades.
options.note: The text describes a sudden wreck, not a gradual economic decline.

options.text: An internal mutiny among her own sailors.
options.note: No mutiny is described; the destructive force named is the east wind, a recognized image for divine judgment.

options.text: A fire that started within the ship itself.
options.note: The specific cause named in the text is the east wind, not an internal fire.

quiz.q: How do the sailors and kings respond to Tyre's wreck, according to verses 29 to 35?

options.text: They abandon ship, cry out bitterly, throw dust on their heads, and are appalled and shaken with fear.
options.note: Verses 29 to 35 describe exactly this range of mourning and dread among sailors and kings alike.

options.text: They quickly rebuild a new ship to replace her.
options.note: No rebuilding effort is described; the response is entirely one of grief and horror.

options.text: They celebrate the removal of a trade competitor.
options.note: The text describes deep mourning and terror, the opposite of celebration.

options.text: They remain calm, viewing it as a routine business loss.
options.note: The described reactions, bitter weeping, dust, shaved heads, are far stronger than a routine, calm response.

quiz.q: What is the chapter's underlying lesson about wealth, beauty, and human achievement?

options.text: Even the most impressive, far reaching human achievement cannot outlast God's judgment when it becomes a source of self sufficient pride.
options.note: Tyre's own boast, 'I am perfect in beauty,' verse 3, is answered by total collapse, tying her pride directly to her fall.

options.text: Wealth and trade are inherently sinful and should be avoided entirely.
options.note: The passage does not condemn trade or craftsmanship itself, but rather the self sufficient pride built upon them.

options.text: Only nations without any natural resources are ever judged by God.
options.note: The opposite is shown; Tyre is judged precisely because of her greatness and pride in her resources and trade.

options.text: Human skill and craftsmanship have no value in God's eyes.
options.note: The chapter describes Tyre's craftsmanship with real appreciation for its detail and skill; the judgment falls on pride, not on skill itself.

questions: Tyre's boast was 'I am perfect in beauty,' built entirely from her own trade and craftsmanship. What accomplishment or possession are you tempted to credit entirely to your own skill rather than to God's provision?

The chapter lingers lovingly over Tyre's genuine skill and global reach before describing her sudden collapse. Where has something genuinely good in your life, a skill, a relationship, a role, quietly become the thing you trust in instead of God?

The east wind wrecked Tyre 'in the heart of the sea,' at the very height of her success. Have you experienced a sudden reversal at a moment when things seemed most secure, and how did that shape your trust in God afterward?

The sailors and kings who once profited from Tyre now mourn her as though she were a person who had died. Who or what in your life have you depended on in ways that, if lost, would leave a grief this deep, and how does that compare to your dependence on God?

Unlike Tyre's trading empire, Christ offers a kingdom that 'cannot be shaken.' What would it look like this week to consciously build your security on Christ rather than on achievements, income, or reputation that could be swept away by a single wind?

translationNotes.note: Tyre's own claim, 'I am perfect in beauty,' uses the Hebrew kalil, complete or whole, a term that elsewhere in Scripture is reserved for describing wholehearted devotion or completeness properly belonging to God, making her boast especially striking.
The BSB text notes uncertainty in the precise identification of some place names in this verse, such as Izal; the general sense of extensive trade in fine goods is not affected.

The closing phrase, 'you have come to a horrible end and will be no more,' matches almost word for word the ending of the lament over the king of Tyre in 28:19, tying this chapter and the next together as a single extended meditation on Tyre's fall.
